title: No place without God
hookLine: Hasidic teaching: no place is empty of God

cards: A man is running from his brother. Night falls somewhere in the open, and he lies down on the ground with a stone under his head. Nowhere special.

Just the spot where the sun went down. He dreams of a ladder, with angels going up and down it, and when he wakes he says: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." The place hadn't changed overnight.
Jacob had. Hasidic teachers made much of that surprise.

teach.b: No place without God. First, the prophet. Isaiah sees the angels calling to one another: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory."
Not the Temple only. The whole earth. Second, the kabbalists' line.

teach.h: NO PLACE IS EMPTY OF HIM.
teach.b: The Tikkunei Zohar, a work in the Zohar's family, says it in Aramaic: leit atar panui minei, there is no place empty of Him. The rabbis even give God a name that means the Place, HaMakom.
And remember tzimtzum, a week ago: if God drew in to make room for a world, is that room empty? The Hasidic reading answers no. The hiding is real.
The emptiness isn't. Third, the street. Hasidic teachers carried the line out of the study house into kitchens, markets and workshops.

teach.h: THE BUS STOP AND THE LAUNDRY.
teach.b: If no place is empty of God, then the bus stop, the laundry pile and the waiting room are not outside holiness. They're places where it's hidden. Fourth, the hard places.
A line like this is easy at sunset and harder in a bad week.
But notice where Jacob found it: on a stone pillow, running for his life.
There is nowhere the sparks fell where God is absent.

how: Hasidic teachers repeat the line that no place is empty of God as a reason to serve God in ordinary life, at work, at meals and on the road, and not only in the synagogue or study house.

games.q: what does “no place without god” mean?
o: the belief that God lives only in the Temple
a rule that prayer can happen in any building
the teaching that no place is empty of God

p: the LORD is in this place
the whole earth is full of His glory
no place is empty of Him
the Place, a name for God

s: in Isaiah, God's glory fills only the Temple
the angels call: the whole earth is full of His glory.
Jacob knew the place was holy before he lay down
he woke and said: surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not.
the Tikkunei Zohar says no place is empty of Him
leit atar panui minei, in its Aramaic.

games.q: you're Jacob, on the run, waking on the ground with a stone for a pillow. what do you say?
o: this place is too ordinary for God.
surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not.
I'll look for God once I reach somewhere safe.
games.why: Jacob says the LORD was in that ordinary place all along; he just hadn't known it.

practice: Look at the place you're in right now, exactly as it is, the chair, the light, the clutter, and let your eyes move slowly from one ordinary thing to the next, holding one simple thought: even here.
If you pray, you can say Jacob's words quietly: surely the LORD is in this place. If you don't, just stay with the place, and let it be enough.

wordCard.voice: No place without God. The Hasidic teaching, drawn from the Tikkunei Zohar, that no place is empty of Him. Today's words.

orig.note: Hebrew: the Place, a rabbinic name for God.

carryVoice: Your line: no place without him. The sink and the sidewalk aren't outside holiness. Back tomorrow, same hill.
